what_it_does: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models work by routing each word to one of many specialized sub-networks; the catch is that all those sub-networks must be stored in memory, making MoE models far too large to fit comfortably in a GPU's fast on-chip memory. Stratum solves this by moving the model's weights into a new kind of memory chip (Monolithic 3D-stackable DRAM, or Mono3D DRAM) that sits right next to a custom math processor, and by predicting which sub-networks a batch of user queries will need so the hottest ones are placed in the memory's fastest layers — achieving up to 8.3x more decoding throughput and 7.7x better energy efficiency than a comparable GPU-only system.
method_in_detail:
The memory problem. In an MoE model, each input token is routed to only 1–2 of dozens of specialist sub-networks (experts), but all experts must be stored somewhere accessible. On a GPU, the fast memory (called HBM — high-bandwidth memory — a chip that stacks multiple memory layers above a logic chip using thick copper pillars called TSVs) cannot hold models like Mixtral 8x7B whose expert weights alone are 95% of the total 47-billion-parameter size. Fetching weights from slower memory kills throughput.

The new memory technology. Mono3D DRAM builds hundreds of memory layers sequentially on a single wafer (like 3D NAND flash storage), then bonds the logic chip directly to the bottom of that stack using copper-to-copper hybrid bonding at 1-micrometer pitch — 10x finer than HBM's TSV pitch. This gives the logic chip far wider internal bandwidth (19–34 TB/s internally vs. HBM's ~800 GB/s external). However, because the memory cells near the top of the tall stack have longer wire runs, they are slower to access than cells near the bottom, creating a natural fast/slow tier structure.

The three key innovations. First, in-memory tiering: Stratum defines 8 tiers within the 1,024-layer DRAM stack and puts frequently used expert weights in the faster (lower) tiers. Second, topic-aware prediction: a lightweight classifier (a 67-million-parameter neural network) reads each incoming query, predicts its topic (math, coding, legal, etc.), and looks up a pre-built table showing which experts are most likely to be activated for that topic. Before each batch, a near-memory row-swap buffer physically relocates the predicted hot experts into fast tiers without involving the GPU. Third, an NMP (near-memory processing, meaning math done inside the memory chip rather than shipping data to a separate processor) processor on the logic die handles the matrix multiplications for both expert computation and attention using a ring-connected set of processing units, each with its own small array of multiply-accumulate hardware and a special-function unit for non-linear operations like the attention normalization step.

The result. Compared to GPU baselines running the same MoE models, Stratum delivers up to 8.29x higher decoding throughput and 7.66x better energy efficiency, measured across OLMoE, Mixtral 8x7B, and LLaMA-4 Scout.
